item.title: Go Daily Question 20250604
item.description:
What does the following code output?

package main

import "fmt"

func f(n int) (r int) {
    defer func() {
        r += n
        recover()
    }()

    var f func()

    defer f()
    
    f = func() {
        r += 2
    }
    return n + 1
}

func main() {
    fmt.Println(f(3))
}
🔑 Solution Analysis:

7

// First execute this code, then r is assigned the value 4
return n+1

// Then it executes, but triggers a panic
defer f()

// Finally it executes, r increases by 3, r=7, then recover(), and the function returns 7
defer func() {
        r += n
        recover()
    }()

item.title: Go Daily Question 129
item.description:
What happens when the following code is executed?

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    ch := make(chan int, 1000)
    go func() {
        for i := 0; i < 10; i++ {
            ch <- i
        }
    }()
    go func() {
        for {
            a, ok := <-ch
            if !ok {
                fmt.Println("close")
                return
            }
            fmt.Println("a: ", a)
        }
    }()
    close(ch)
    fmt.Println("ok")
    time.Sleep(time.Second * 100)
}
🔑 Answer Analysis: 
ok
close
panic: send on closed channel

goroutine 6 [running]:

Writing data to a closed channel will cause a panic. Reading data from a closed channel, when there’s no buffered data, will read the zero value.

item.title: Go Daily Question 100
item.description:
What is the output of the following code?

package main

import "fmt"

func f(n int) (r int) {
    defer func() {
        r += n
        recover()
    }()

    var f func()

    defer f()
    
    f = func() {
        r += 2
    }
    return n + 1
}

func main() {
    fmt.Println(f(3))
}
🔑 Answer Analysis:

7

// This code is executed first, then r is assigned 4
return n+1

// Then execute, but it will trigger a panic
defer f()

// Finally, execute, r is incremented by 3 again (r=7), then recover(), and finally the function returns 7
defer func() {
        r += n
        recover()
    }()

item.title: Go Daily Question 095
item.description:
Output of the following code:

package main

import "sync"

func main() {
    var wg sync.WaitGroup
    foo := make(chan int)
    bar := make(chan int)
    wg.Add(1)
    go func() {
        defer wg.Done()
        select {
        case foo <- <-bar:
        default:
            println("default")
        }
    }()
    wg.Wait()
}

A: default B: panic

🔑 Answer Analysis:

Conventionally, one might expect the default branch of the select statement in go func to execute, and the program to run normally. However, the result is not that, but a deadlock. You can test this via: https://play.studygolang.com/p/kF4pOjYXbXf.

item.title: Go Daily Question 050
item.description:
What is the output of the following code?

func main() {  
    s := make(map[string]int)
    delete(s, "h")
    fmt.Println(s["h"])
}

A. runtime panic B. 0 C. compilation error

🔑 Answer Analysis:

B 0 Deleting a non-existent key will not cause a panic. Outputting a non-existent key will return the zero value of its type.

Extension:

func main() {
    var s map[string]int
    delete(s, "h")
    s["h"] = 1
    fmt.Println(s["h"])
}

Deleting from a nil map will also not panic. However, writing to a nil map will panic.

item.title: Go Daily Question 040
item.description:
What is the output of the following code?

type person struct {  
    name string
}

func main() {  
    var m map[person]int
    p := person{"mike"}
    fmt.Println(m[p])
}

A.0 B.1 C.Compilation error

🔑 Answer Analysis:

Answer: A 0

m is a map, and its value is nil. Getting a value from a nil map will not cause an error; instead, it returns the corresponding zero value. Here, the value is of type int, so it returns 0.

item.title: Go Daily Question 037
item.description:
What happens when the following code is executed?

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    ch := make(chan int, 1000)
    go func() {
        for i := 0; i < 10; i++ {
            ch <- i
        }
    }()
    go func() {
        for {
            a, ok := <-ch
            if !ok {
                fmt.Println("close")
                return
            }
            fmt.Println("a: ", a)
        }
    }()
    close(ch)
    fmt.Println("ok")
    time.Sleep(time.Second * 100)
}
🔑 Answer Analysis:

Answer: Prints “ok” then panics. It takes time to start goroutines. Here, the close(ch) statement closes the channel. Writing data to an already closed channel will cause a program panic.

item.title: Go Daily Question 002
item.description:
What is the output of the following code?

package main

import (
    "fmt"
)

func main() {
    defer_call()
}

func defer_call() {
    defer func() { fmt.Println("before print") }()
    defer func() { fmt.Println("during print") }()
    defer func() { fmt.Println("after print") }()

    panic("trigger panic")
}
🔑 Answer Analysis: 
after print
during print
before print
panic: trigger panic

Analysis: The execution order of defer is Last-In, First-Out (LIFO). When a panic statement occurs, defer functions are executed in LIFO order, and finally the panic is executed.
